Later today we are having a firm-wide trader meeting at @smbcapital. A few teams and a couple handful of traders have been struggling. This aligns with what I’m hearing from other desks as well as those on the retail side.

Only fair for me to highlight both the successes AND the struggles of the traders I work with as I try to convey the authentic truth of being a trader.

On the SMB call we will discuss what has been working well, what hasn’t been, and how best to adapt. Soliciting feedback across teams and individuals.

Here is the main message I will be conveying to their traders which I think is useful for all to hear:

IMO, the most common issues I’m seeing is that traders are getting overly involved and over-allocating risk to situations that had potential but never unfolded optimally.

$BWET is a name that got extended, but never enough to take a real stand.

The breakouts in $QQQ or certain single-stock names had solid charts but the breadth beneath the market was awful. We still had yellow lights flashing in certain areas.

The recent AI sell-off was extended and had its moments, but it lacked the intraday flush or intraday setups to size into anything.

When these setups have unfolded suboptimally, traders have continued to stay involved and allocate risk in a refusal to acknowledge that the setup is not as good as it had the potential to be.

I’d argue this comes down to maintaining an objectively high level of subjectivity. Selectivity is staying in your lane and waiting for the setups in your playbook that match the current regime.

Unlike w poker, nothing is forcing you to play or to take a subpar setup. Essentially, you have a good hand and want to place a bet, but if the flop pans out suboptimally, you fold. A lot of traders have not been emotionally willing to fold and not play the hand.

Good trading is recognizing that there might be some positive signs, but then avoiding or sizing down when it doesn't fully line up.

I'd like to share a little about what I've been working on at my new company @ultrametricai with my cofounder @tylerlastovich. We have been exploring how we could automate the startup itself, leaving founders with more time to focus on their exact mission.

Enter our first release of the Open Startup Repo: https://github.com/ultrametricai/ultrametric

A common foundation for transparent automation of the startup. 

After close to 20 years in silicon valley, backing hundreds of amazing founders & startups, being in the trenches of founding Heyzap (YC08), then solo founding @golden, going through 2 acquisitions and working behind the scenes with some of the iconic companies today, I'm witnessing the largest change to how we work I could have imagined - a truly monumental era of creative abundance. 

I believe the next generation of companies will largely run themselves: from operations, code, product upgrades, growth, vendor control & selection, process execution, special situations, strategy etc etc. That leaves founder time for 'the art' at the very niche core: the (currently) unautomatable, the special leaps humans tend to make, and north star setting.

We want founders to go super deep into the main problem they are trying to solve and not get held up doing anything else, from searching for domain availability with trademark checks to setting their company up, to running their processes on autopilot. 

So to help that broad foundational layer for starting and running a company, we have spent around a year exploring how to help founders focus on their mission across different verticals, geos, stages and initial starting conditions.

Our first few attempts at making something useful actually failed as the market and AI was moving so fast; it just got absorbed into the models or other product releases. We saw polsia happen, openclaw, then grokbot, muse, dots, etc era as the astras, fables, opuses, kimis and jevs rolled out. What seemed to have been missing along the way was a common repo to identify, unify, open and normalize all the lego bricks that startups have to interact with (vendors, processes, business logic, law, best practices, surface areas, art of the possible). 

As the number of software vendors blew up, the interfaces to drive them multiplied, the international startup founder blew up as silicon valley moved from a specific location to a state of mind and global movement. Unlimited pre seed funding in unlimited vertical sub markets and permutations has brought us to the age of infinity but we have yet to achieve being able to type into an agent a very simple sentence with very complex implications 'just setup my company and make $1m/m'. We have ended up with a hybrid mismash of computer use, API calls, plugins, shifting surface areas (API/MCP/CLI/plugins/chats/musish futures), and changing model absorption to vendor balance making it an exciting and unstable time. 

As our first step we started to rank all the vendors that startups interface to when going about their journey in terms of how agentically controllable they are via their APIs, MCPs, CLIs etc and computer use compatibility as we are largely switching from a UI driven world to the agentic control surfaces and onto full automation. We have 100 ranking areas you can check out with an overall open ranking here: https://ultrametric.ai/overall

Then we looked at the processes that startups do and how the vendors rank for the sub steps or process as a whole and how this changes across geos. Open processes: https://ultrametric.ai/processes

Then we started to hack on an open repo for startups that would contain all the components we are going to need for a common foundation for founders across the globe even if our gov processes vary so much from Bengaluru to SF or Lisbon to Shenzhen.  The founder spirit is geo-invariant. 

We have looked at special founder/startup situations, the business logic that will make open modules for the startup that we can hack on

The 10 Year Treasury Is Looking Beyond Inflation And Seeing Something Much Worse

The U.S. 10 year Treasury yield plunged roughly 18 basis points to 4.965%. The story is not just the size of the move. It is what rallied alongside bonds, what sold off, and where investors were buying.

The Signal Inside The Yield Curve

The strongest declines were in 5 and 7 year maturities, down about 19 basis points, versus 14 at 30 years and fewer than 5 at 3 months. I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus.

The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future.

I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf.

Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.

Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.

Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.

Why now

We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.

But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.

This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.

More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.

I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.

Believing before consensus

My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.

I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.

I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”

Then we work backward together to make it happen.

In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.

Bond returns have become positively correlated with equity returns. And I expect that relationship to persist for one simple reason: bonds themselves have become a risky asset.

But that doesn't mean bonds will magically return to being a low-risk asset class offering decent positive returns and meaningful diversification.

Quite the contrary.

Pension funds and other investors abandoning French government bonds further confirm that the nature of bonds has fundamentally changed.

And when yields eventually decline, as I expect they will, won't the reason be yet another reminder that bonds need central bank support to prevent actual defaults?

I think so.

And in that environment, can you think of other asset classes that would benefit even more from that support than the bonds themselves?

We can!

That's why we build robust, long-term investment portfolios without traditional bonds, but with scarce assets such as gold.

Here are the most important highlights from @Tesla's Q3 2026 earnings call:

• Tesla's 2027 Megapack production capacity is nearly sold out.

• Tesla is aiming to produce 5 million vehicles annually by 2030.

• Customers are increasingly visiting Tesla showrooms specifically to experience FSD rather than shopping for a particular vehicle model.

• Tesla said more than 75% of new North American vehicle deliveries included a paid FSD subscription signup, despite every vehicle already coming with a free one-month trial.

• FSD financial disclosure: Tesla plans to disclose additional FSD financial and operating metrics as the business scales, including subscription revenue and churn rates.

• Elon said Tesla is hoping for EU-wide FSD approval within a few months and would be surprised if approval takes longer than Q1 2027, although the timing depends on regulators.

• Unsupervised FSD for customer vehicles: Tesla expects to enable some customer-owned vehicles to participate in its autonomous Robotaxi network around Q2 2027, subject to fleet-management and geofencing requirements.

• Tesla is developing its own AI-based mapping and navigation system that will rely on intelligence gathered from its vehicle fleet rather than traditional third-party mapping systems. The system will support conversational voice commands, personalized routing preferences, improved parking, and more intelligent destination handling.

•  Tesla plans to launch Cybercab service in Dallas in November 2026, followed by additional cities.

• Tesla plans to progressively extend robotaxi operating hours, with the goal of reaching 24/7 service by the end of 2026. Tesla expects to expand service to highways, higher-speed roads, additional weather conditions, and nighttime operations by the end of 2026.

• Elon expects Robotaxi to begin making a noticeable contribution to Tesla's financial results around Q2 2027, potentially becoming a significant business by Q3 or Q4 2027.

• Tesla is targeting the first deliveries of Cybercabs to fleet owner customers by the end of 2026, but Elon said the vast majority of Cybercabs will be Tesla-owned and operated as transportation-as-a-service vehicles rather than sold directly to consumers.

• Tesla has started early Optimus production. Elon said: "The growth of Optimus is an S curve, but the initial curve is a shallow slope. There's still some things we need to tweak about the design. There's still quite a lot of work to do with the AI in the robot. I would expect that the AI, the electromechanical design, reliability, usage life, expect these issues to be solved by the end of next year."

• Elon said most of the equipment for an Optimus production line designed to manufacture approximately 1 million robots annually is already at Fremont. Elon expects it will take at least another year, possibly longer, to reach an annualized production rate of approximately 1 million Optimus robots, equivalent to roughly 20,000 per week.

• Elon said Tesla may release a new Optimus V3 demonstration video within one or two months, saying  that it should show genuinely AI-driven tasks rather than preprogrammed movements.

• Tesla is targeting mid-2027 to integrate its AI5 chip into Optimus.

• Management said Optimus production costs are trending toward the expected manufacturing cost of Cybercab, although the robot's design is still being refined.

• Tesla hopes to manufacture its first experimental semiconductor chips around May or June 2027. Tesla is targeting useful chip production at volume in Terafab around Q3 2028.

• Management expects higher Megapack average selling prices and further improvements in gross margins (currently 33%) as production expands.

I didn't predict and do not predict defense running ahead of offense automatically. I predict cybersecurity will be endgame defense-favoring but the transition will be hard. In particular, "good guys find vulns in already-released software before the bad guys do" is not a defense-favoring game. Making the game defense-favoring requires deeper shifts in methodology including formal verification, aggressive TCB minimization, etc, and we've only barely started making those transitions.

One market. One setup. One risk framework. And don’t touch anything else for a year.

Stop watching every candle. Stop clicking buttons. Follow the plan and let the trade run according to the plan.

4. Find someone to hold you accountable.

A mentor, a partner, a community. Someone who acts as your manager, coach and reality check all at once. Be comfortable making progress alone… but don’t shut out opportunities that help you hit your goals faster.
